newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian oil output recovery masks serious problems.
newsitem.headline: Russian oil output recovery masks serious problems.

text.p: Russia's oil sector, the world's third largest, has hit a milestone -- but on paper only.
Half-year figures showing output stable for the first time in a decade mask an array of serious problems ahead.

Russian crude oil production hit 5.88 million barrels per day over the first half of 1997, according to official data earlier this week, a rise of 0.4 percent on year-ago levels and the first time since 1987 that output has not declined.
But the long-awaited turnaround may not be sustainable without big and fairly immediate structural changes.

"Our whole future is in the North, but these are precisely the reserves not being tapped," said energy expert Alexei Kocheshkov of AssoSPneft, a Moscow-based producers' group. "All the other reserves in Russia are at the bottom of the barrel."

Russia, eking out the last drops of oil from fields with precious few years of commercial productivity left, has neither the money, infrastructure nor legislation needed to attract money for the remote reserves upon which its future depends.
"We could spend another two years not tapping the hard-to-recovers and keep output flat," Kocheshkov said. "But after that, we would see a cycle of decline set in again."
Russian oil output has shrunk by over half since its 1987 peak of 11.47 million bpd, with double digit drops in the first years of this decade levelling off only last year.
Now the sector is in a new but no less difficult era.

After output of cheap and easy oil shrank because of a lack of technology to handle hard-to-recover oil, macro-economic factors set in, with producers pumping the smaller volumes Russia's shrinking economy needed in the early 1990s when reforms began.
Producers, many of them now vertically-integrated companies accountable to shareholders, see imminent economic growth and export revenues on the horizon and want to produce more oil.
Domestic crude prices, near world levels, and strong world oil prices may have fuelled the first-half recovery, analysts said.
But capital investment in production is at most half the $2 billion a year the World Bank says is needed to maintain output at current levels over 10 years.

Hard-to-recover reserves in the energy-rich North, which includes the Yamal Peninsula, Timan-Pechora and Barents and Kara Seas fields, account for up to 60 percent of Russia's total reserves. But they cost up to 40 percent more to tap.

They are hardly being touched. West Siberian and northern production sharing deals with foreign firms are on hold over flawed legislation. South Siberian oil, in Irkutsk, will stay untouched until pipelines and other infrastructure are built.

Another problem is Russia's approach to associated gas, a hydrocarbon it simply flares into the air as worthless material but which is heavily present in northern reserves and must be gathered to make oil output there economical.
If LUKoil, Russia's biggest and most successful oil company, is a barometer of the sector's state, the picture is not pretty.

LUKoil is one of Russia's promptest and biggest corporate tax payers and has a strategic, cash-accessing alliance with ARCO. But it is pouring its investment dollars into Caspian, not Russian, projects.

"That should be a very serious sign something has to change," said a senior Western energy source. "If not, I would expect the overall decline to resume, and in five to 10 years it could become quite serious."

Moscow is already moving to revoke exploration and production licences from regions and companies which are simply sitting on them. But it is also considering raising the excise tariffs producers pay on output by an average 30 percent, which could kill any plans to boost output.
"I'm only cautiously optimistic," Kocheshkov said. "Russian oil is like a sick man after an operation -- you have to see if he pulls through long-term."
